name: Akkadian
blurb: The language of Hammurabi's laws and the Epic of Gilgamesh, and the earliest written Semitic language.
facts: Akkadian is named after Akkad, the capital of Sargon's empire around 2300 BC.
It is the earliest written Semitic language, a distant cousin of Hebrew and Arabic.
In the 14th century BC Egyptian pharaohs corresponded with Near Eastern kings in Akkadian. The letters were found at Amarna.
In 1857 four scholars translated the same newly found inscription separately. Their versions agreed, and cuneiform was declared deciphered.
Hammurabi's law code is carved on a black stone stele over two metres tall, now in the Louvre.
The last known cuneiform tablets are astronomical almanacs from the first century AD.

guide.p: Cuneiform means 'wedge-shaped'. Scribes pressed a reed stylus into wet clay. Akkadian borrowed the script from the Sumerians.
Most signs write a syllable: a vowel (a), consonant + vowel (ba) or vowel + consonant (an, um). Words are spelled sign by sign, and we put hyphens between the signs.
a-wi-lum is read awīlum. The spelling rarely shows vowel length, so the macrons come from the dictionary, not the tablet.
A sign can have several values. 𒀭 is the syllable an, but also DINGIR 'god'. Readings in capitals are whole words, which you will meet in unit 3.

guide.p: Nouns end in -um as the subject, -am as the object and -im after 'of' and after prepositions.
The final -m is called mimation. Later Akkadian dropped it (awīlu), but Old Babylonian keeps it.
Feminine nouns add -t-: mārum 'son', mārtum 'daughter'; aḫum 'brother', aḫātum 'sister'.
Put two nouns side by side to say 'X is Y'. ul 'not' goes before the part it denies.
ex: the man is not a slave

guide.p: The first noun drops its ending and the second takes -im: mārum becomes mār, aššatum becomes aššat, mārtum becomes mārat.

guide.p: Common words are often written with one Sumerian sign read in Akkadian: LUGAL is šarrum, É is bītum. The case ending is not written, so É can be bītum, bītam or bītim.
Before a god's name the DINGIR sign is silent and marks it as divine; we write it ᵈ. After a place name the sign KI 'place' does the same.
An adjective comes after its noun and copies its ending.

To say 'is strong', Akkadian uses the stative: the adjective without any ending. So šarrum dannum is 'the strong king', but šarrum dan is 'the king is strong'. This course uses the stative for every 'is' + adjective.

units.title: Iprus
units.about: Verbs, the past and the present

guide.p: Akkadian order is subject, object, verb. The object takes -am.
Verbs are built on roots like p-r-s 'decide'. The preterite iprus is the simple past, 'he decided'. The present iparras is 'he decides' or 'he will decide'.
A prefix shows the person: i- 'he' or 'she', a- 'I'. anāku 'I' is added only for emphasis.
Some everyday verbs bend the pattern: illik 'he went', illak 'he goes'; iddin 'he gave', inaddin 'he gives'.

items.note: Send a person or a message; so also 'write to'.

guide.p: Letters were read aloud to the addressee, so they begin 'to X say: thus says Y'. -ma closes each part.
li- turns a verb into a wish. A blessing often follows the opening.
Each law is a case: šumma 'if' and the crime in the preterite, then the penalty in the present. English puts the crime in the present: 'if a man steals'. Here u means 'or'.
-ma links two clauses: īpušma is 'he built, and then'.

The laws are quoted from the Codex Hammurabi stele: § 6 (theft from a god or palace), § 21 (breaking into a house) and § 229 (a builder whose house collapses and kills its owner). umma Ḫammurapīma opens Hammurabi's letter to Sîn-iddinam (AbB 2 33). Šamaš liballiṭka is the standard greeting, as in VS 16 109.

units.title: Iptaras
units.about: Past, present and perfect: the G-stem in full

guide.p: Every verb has three main forms. Built on p-r-s 'decide': iprus 'he decided' (preterite), iparras 'he decides' or 'he will decide' (present) and iptaras 'he has decided' (perfect).
The perfect puts -ta- after the first root consonant. It means 'has done'. Letters use it for news that has just happened, and in a chain of past events it marks the last, decisive step.
ex: now he has sent a tablet

guide.h: Each verb has its own vowels
guide.p: The vowel before the last consonant changes from verb to verb, so learn the past and present together: išpur and išappar, iṣbat and iṣabbat, imqut and imaqqut. Dictionaries list verbs by the infinitive: šapārum 'to send', ṣabātum 'to seize', maqātum 'to fall'.

Prefixes show who acts: i- 'he' or 'she', ta- 'you', a- 'I', ni- 'we'. Plurals add an ending: i-...-ū 'they' (men or mixed), i-...-ā 'they' (women), ta-...-ā 'you all'. Speaking to a woman, 'you' adds -ī: tašpurī.
Masculine nouns drop the mimation and end in -ū as subject and -ī elsewhere: ilū 'the gods', ana ilī 'to the gods'. Feminines lengthen the vowel before -t-: šarratum 'queen', šarrātum 'queens'.
ex: the men went to the palace

items.note: The long -ū is not written: iš-pu-ru.

units.title: Uballiṭ
units.about: The D and Š stems: make it so, make it happen

guide.p: A root can be put into several stems that shift its meaning. The plain one is the G-stem. The D-stem doubles the middle consonant and the Š-stem adds š. Both use the prefix u- for 'he' and 'I', tu- for 'you' and nu- for 'we'.
uparris (past), uparras (present), uptarris (perfect). It often turns a quality into an action: damqum 'good' gives udammiq 'he made good', danānum 'be strong' gives udannin 'he made strong'.
liballiṭka 'may he keep you well' in letters is the D-stem of balāṭum 'to live'. In the Hammurabi story, uḫtappid 'he has blinded' is a D perfect.

ušapris (past), ušapras (present), uštapris (perfect). It means 'make someone or something do it': maqātum 'fall' gives ušamqit 'he made fall, he struck down', ḫalāqum 'perish' gives ušaḫliq 'he destroyed'.
Kings described their wars with Š-stems: they struck down armies and destroyed cities. ummān nakrim is 'the army of the enemy', with ummānum in its short bound form.
ex: the king struck down the enemy's army

items.note: D-stem of danānum 'to be strong'. Compare dannum.

guide.p: Tablets write numbers with wedges: an upright wedge for each one, a corner wedge for each ten. The spoken words behind them are often uncertain, so scholars write numbers as digits.
Babylonian counting went up in sixties, as our minutes and hours still do. The wedge for 1 also stands for 60, and the reader tells which from context.
Silver was weighed out, not counted. 60 šiqlū 'shekels' (about 8 grams each) made a manûm 'mina' (about half a kilo), and 60 minas made a biltum 'talent'.
Barley, šeʾum, was measured by volume. A kurrum 'kor' held 300 qû, roughly 300 litres. Silver and barley both served as money.
The measure takes a short fixed form (šiqil, mana, kur) and the goods follow in whatever case the sentence needs.
ex: he shall pay one mina of silver

guide.p: šâmum 'to buy' has the past išām. 'From' the seller is itti. To sell is to 'give for silver', ana kaspim nadānum.
ex: he bought barley from the merchant

guide.p: 1 mana kaspam išaqqal is Hammurabi's law § 198. The merchant loan comes from § 49, and selling a field 'for silver' from § 40.

guide.p: ša opens a relative clause. The clause follows its noun, and its verb still comes last.
ex: the man who built the house

guide.p: In a subordinate clause a verb ending in a consonant adds -u: īpuš becomes īpušu, iddin becomes iddinu. Forms that already end in a vowel, like išpurū 'they sent', stay as they are.
ex: the silver which the man gave

guide.p: The noun can also drop its ending and run straight into the clause. Hammurabi's builder law says bīt īpušu 'the house he built'. The Gilgameš epic opens ša naqba īmuru, 'he who saw the Deep', with īmuru in the subjunctive.
inūma 'when', ištu 'after', adi 'until' and aššum 'because' also put the verb in the subjunctive. Before a noun, aššum means 'concerning'.
ex: when the king went to Babylon

guide.p: Subordinate clauses and šumma clauses use lā for 'not'. ul is for main clauses.
ex: aššum bīt īpušu lā udanninuma imqutu

guide.p: šumma 'if' does not take the subjunctive: šumma awīlum bītam ipluš, not iplušu.

guide.p: The imperative comes from the 'you' form of the past without its prefix, with a vowel added to begin it: tašpur 'you sent' gives šupur 'send!', taškun gives šukun 'place!', taṣbat gives ṣabat 'seize!'.
Common verbs are irregular: alik 'go!', idin 'give!', qibi 'say!'. To a woman add -ī (šuprī), to a group -ā (šuprā).
The precative turns the past into a wish: li- for 'he' or 'she' (liddin 'let him give'), lu- for 'I' (lušpur 'let me send') and li-...-ū for 'they'.
ex: let me write to my lord

guide.p: For D and Š verbs, li- replaces the u-: uballiṭ becomes liballiṭ. -ka adds 'you': liballiṭka 'may he keep you well', liballiṭūka 'may they keep you well'.
lū before a stative makes a wish. šalim 'he is well' becomes šalmāta 'you are well', so lū šalmāta is 'may you be well'.
ex: may you be well, may you be healthy

guide.p: A prohibition is lā with the present 'you' form: lā tallak 'do not go'. lā tašappar 'do not send'.
After the address and the blessing the writer comes to the point, often with anumma 'herewith' or aššum 'concerning'. Requests are imperatives, and promises use lu-.

items.note: Stative of šalāmum 'to be well', for 'you'.

guide.p: Babylonian poems are built from lines in two halves that echo each other, as in Atrahasis: dullum kabit, mād šapšāqum, 'the toil was heavy, the hardship great'. Word order is freer than in prose.
The flood story opens when the gods themselves had to dig the canals: inūma ilū awīlum. Lambert read awīlum as 'like men'; von Soden read it as 'were man'. Scholars still disagree.
ex: when the gods were like men

guide.p: The first Akkadian epic of Gilgameš was composed in Old Babylonian times. Around 1200 BC it was reworked into the Standard Babylonian epic of twelve tablets, which tells the flood story in Tablet XI. That later dialect drops mimation and blurs the case endings: šarru for šarrum.
The bārûm 'diviner' read the liver of a sacrificed sheep. Each omen is a šumma sentence: what he saw, then the prediction in the present. Collections listed hundreds of them.
ex: the prince will fall on the campaign he goes on

guide.p: A t or d before -šu merges with it into ss: qāt + šu gives qāssu. 'His hand will reach' means 'he will conquer'.
ex: the king will conquer his enemy's land

guide.p: inūma ilū awīlum and dullum kabit are Atrahasis OB I 1 and 4 (BM 78941). ša naqba īmuru is Gilgameš SB I 1. The omens come from the Yale Old Babylonian omen tablets YOS 10 17 and YOS 10 42.
